code: House Bill 1009 · 2026 · became law as Act 395
title: Georgia lawmakers ban school-day phone use in public high schools by July 1, 2027
linkText: Phones in Georgia public high schools (House Bill 1009)

status.text: High school ban starts by July 1, 2027

disclosure: Drafted with AI help from the archived sources below. Every sentence links to its source or is labeled as our analysis. Checked by automated tests and independent AI reviewers. This is a test page; no person reviewed it.

units.t: House Bill (HB) 1009 will bar public high school students from accessing phones, smartwatches, tablets and similar devices during the school day, unless a disability or medical plan explicitly requires it, or another law does.
Georgia lawmakers and the governor approved the law.
Public high school students, their families and school staff.
High schools must start the ban by July 1, 2027.
Districts set the details.
Ask your district about its rules, or tell lawmakers whether to keep or change the law.
units.note: suggested actions; districts set policies each year under P-008, and the General Assembly can amend laws in later sessions

blocks.label: If you're a student at a Georgia public high school

units.t: By July 1, 2027, you can't access phones or similar devices during the school day.
Exceptions: only the access your disability or medical plan explicitly requires, or another law requires.
units.note: P-013 allows the access a student's IEP, Section 504 plan or medical plan explicitly requires, "as necessary to fulfill the requirements" of that plan, and P-007 allows access "required by law"; "disability plan" is our plain-language term for an IEP or Section 504 plan, not from the cited sources

units.t: Not known as of Nov 8, 2026: when your school will start the ban.
units.note: P-007 sets "no later than July 1, 2027", P-008 makes policies due by January 1 each year, and the law doesn't say how the two dates fit; one school's plan (P-054) is the only one in our sources

blocks.label: If your child attends a Georgia public high school

units.t: By July 1, 2027, reaching your child during the school day means contacting the school; staff must coordinate all emergency messages.
Not known as of Nov 8, 2026: who pays for phone storage (the law sets aside no money; we didn't review the state budget).
units.note: each district chooses storage (P-009); no funding or fee provision in the law's full text, P-001 to P-019 and P-056 to P-061; any state funding would come through the state budget, which is outside our sources

blocks.label: If you work at a Georgia public high school

units.t: By July 1, 2027, your school must enforce the phone ban, which may include assigning staff and checking phone storage.
Not known as of Nov 8, 2026: how much work enforcement takes; the law sets aside no money, and we didn't review the state budget.
units.note: no district's policy is in our sources; no funding provision in the law's full text, P-001 to P-019 and P-056 to P-061; any state funding would come through the state budget, which is outside our sources

blocks.label: If your child is in kindergarten through 8th grade at a Georgia public school

units.t: HB 1009 keeps House Bill 340's school-day device ban for public school students in kindergarten through 8th grade.
The bill drops e-readers from its incomplete list of example devices and requires yearly policies.
Not known as of Nov 8, 2026: your district's next policy.
units.note: P-008 requires a policy by January 1 each year; no district's policy is in our sources

subs.title: Decided now, and decided later

units.t: The law takes effect Dec 31, 2026.
From then on, each district's and school's device policy, due by January 1 each year, must cover kindergarten through 12th grade; the first deadline is Jan 1, 2027.
units.note: P-008 sets "By January 1 each year" for policies covering kindergarten through grade twelve, and the law takes effect Dec 31, 2026 (P-019)

units.t: High schools must start the ban no later than July 1, 2027, so the ban must be in place by the 2027-28 school year.
units.note: P-007 sets "no later than July 1, 2027"; a news report put the start in the 2027-28 school year (P-072)

units.t: The law doesn't say how the January policy deadline fits with the July start date.
units.note: the full enacted text (P-001 to P-019, P-056 to P-061) sets both dates (P-008, P-007) without linking them

blocks.label: Decided by the law, the rule

units.t: The ban covers personal phones, smartwatches, tablets, headphones and similar devices, but schools can still give students laptops and tablets for schoolwork.
Under the law, to "access" a device means to view, hold, wear or otherwise use it, for things like messages, going online, games or music.
The ban lasts from the first bell to the last, including breaks and time between classes, a period the law calls "bell-to-bell."
Breaking the rule brings consequences that grow each time, such as warnings, taking the device or notifying parents.
Charter schools and other schools that can usually skip some state rules can't skip this one.
A student may access a device that their Individualized Education Program (IEP), Section 504 plan or medical plan explicitly requires.
That access is allowed only "as necessary to fulfill the requirements" of the plan.
IEP and Section 504 plans are formal school plans for students with disabilities.
units.note: plain-language definition, not from the cited sources

units.t: Access that another law requires is also allowed.

blocks.label: Decided later by each school district

units.t: Each district and public school sets the details in a policy, which it must adopt, and revise as needed, by January 1 each year.
The details include where phones are kept, such as lockers or locked pouches, and rules for field trips, school transportation and sports.
Each district's or school's code of conduct sets the exact consequences.

blocks.label: Decided later by the General Assembly

units.t: Georgia's lawmakers, the General Assembly, can change the law in a later session.
units.note: the General Assembly can amend laws in later sessions

subs.title: Not known yet

blocks.label: When your child's high school starts the ban

units.t: The ban must start no later than July 1, 2027.
Policies are due by January 1 each year.
The law doesn't say how the two dates fit.
units.note: the full enacted text (P-001 to P-019, P-056 to P-061) sets both dates (P-007, P-008) without linking them

units.t: Our sources include only one school's plan, as of Nov 8, 2026.
units.note: P-054 is the only school plan in our sources

blocks.label: What happens at your school when a student breaks the rule

units.t: The law gives examples, such as warnings or taking the device, but each district's or school's code of conduct sets the exact steps, and we haven't reviewed any code of conduct, as of Nov 8, 2026.
units.note: P-012 gives the examples and leaves the steps to each code of conduct; no code of conduct is in our sources

blocks.label: Where phones will be kept, and whether that costs families anything

units.t: Each district chooses how phones are stored, the law doesn't say who pays, and we haven't seen any district's choice, as of Nov 8, 2026.
units.note: P-009; no funding or fee provision in the law's full text, P-001 to P-019 and P-056 to P-061

blocks.label: What the law will cost the state and districts

units.t: We found no official cost estimate, called a fiscal note, on the state's list for 2026 bills, as of Nov 8, 2026.
units.note: the list's whole 2026 section (P-069) has no entry for HB 1009

units.t: Costs also depend on each district's choices, such as lockers or locked pouches.
units.note: storage options are listed in P-009

blocks.label: Whether the ban will change learning, well-being or safety

units.t: High schools must start the ban no later than July 1, 2027, and we found no measured results from Georgia high schools, as of Nov 8, 2026.
units.note: P-007; none in the sources reviewed, though a state senator said limits had been used in high schools already (P-046) and one school planned to start in 2026-2027 (P-054)

subs.title: What you can do

units.t: Ask your school district how it will store phones, handle emergency messages, run off-campus activities and respond when students break the rules.
units.note: suggested action; districts set these under P-009, P-010, P-011 and P-012

units.t: Each district and public school must adopt or update its policy by January 1 each year.
If your district holds a family workshop, question-and-answer session or town hall, you can ask your questions there.
units.note: suggested action

units.t: The law encourages districts and schools to hold such events.
Tell state lawmakers in the General Assembly what you think of the law, whether you want it kept or changed.
units.note: suggested action; the General Assembly can amend laws in later sessions

units.t: Check your school's handbook or website, where each district and school must publish the rules.

subs.title: Who decides, and how to reach them

units.t: Georgia's lawmakers, in the House and the Senate, passed HB 1009 in 2026.
The General Assembly can change the law in a later session.
units.note: the General Assembly can amend laws in later sessions

units.t: Our sources give no phone number, email or meeting for lawmakers.
units.note: none of the archived sources lists one; the General Assembly's lawmaker lookup page held no readable text when we tried to save it on Nov 8, 2026

units.t: Gov. Brian Kemp signed HB 1009 into law on May 5, 2026.
To reach the governor's office, call (404) 656-1776 or write to 206 Washington Street, Suite 203, State Capitol, Atlanta, GA 30334.

blocks.label: Each school district and public school

units.t: Each district and public school sets the details in a policy, which it must adopt, and revise as needed, by January 1 each year.
The law calls a district a "local school system."
The rules must appear in student and family handbooks, codes of conduct and school websites.
The law encourages districts and schools to hold family workshops, question-and-answer sessions and town halls.
Our sources give no phone numbers or emails for districts.
units.note: none of the archived sources lists one for any district; we found no state directory of districts to save on Nov 8, 2026

subs.title: Coming up

units.t: The law takes effect.
Each school district and public school must adopt its device policy, revising it as needed, to cover kindergarten through 12th grade.
The first such deadline under the new law is Jan 1, 2027.
units.note: P-008 sets "January 1 each year" and the law takes effect Dec 31, 2026 (P-019)

units.t: Public high schools must start the ban.
At least one school planned to start sooner: on June 1, 2026, Cairo High School said it would begin in the 2026-2027 school year.
The Georgia Department of Education must give schools guidance and technical support.

subs.title: What happened

units.t: The bill was filed in the House.
A House committee on education recommended passing the bill.
The House passed the bill, 145 to 20.
A Senate committee on children and families recommended passing the bill.
Senators voted down, 13 to 38, a change that would have let districts allow high school students to access phones between classes.
The Senate passed the bill, 52 to 0.
The governor signed the bill into law as Act 395.
Act 395 is the law's number; HB 1009 was the bill's number.
units.note: plain-language note; P-024 gives Act 395, and P-028 and P-054 give the bill number

units.t: Whether to extend Georgia's school-day device ban for public schools from kindergarten through 8th grade to high school.

blocks.label: How the law describes distraction-free education

units.t: A learning environment where student access to personal devices is banned "to minimize distractions, improve academic outcomes, and increase meaningful interactions and focused learning experiences."
A 2025 law, House Bill 340, already bars device access during the school day for public school students in kindergarten through 8th grade.
That rule had to start no later than July 1, 2026.
The rules that already cover younger students in public schools will apply through 12th grade.
Starting no later than July 1, 2027, students won't be allowed to access devices during the school day.
The ban covers phones, smartwatches, tablets, headphones and similar devices.
To "access" a device means to view, hold, wear or otherwise use it, for things like messages, going online, games or music.
The school day runs from the first bell to the last, including breaks and time between classes, a period the law calls "bell-to-bell."
Each school district and public school chooses where phones go, such as lockers, locked pouches or a set place in the classroom.
The law calls a school district a "local school system."
Parents who need to reach their child during the school day must contact the school.
In an emergency, school staff coordinate all messages through the school's emergency systems.
Because the law says "all," the rule covers messages from the school and between families and students.
units.note: P-011 covers "all emergency communication"

units.t: Students whose IEP (Individualized Education Program), Section 504 plan or medical plan explicitly requires a device may access it as the plan requires.
IEP and Section 504 plans are formal school plans for students with disabilities.
units.note: plain-language definition, not from the cited sources

units.t: Access that another law requires is also allowed.
Breaking the rules leads to consequences that grow with each violation, such as warnings, taking the device, notifying parents and other actions.
Each district's or school's code of conduct sets the exact steps.

subs.title: Also new in this law

units.t: Once the law takes effect on Dec 31, 2026, each school district and public school must adopt its policy, revising it as needed, by January 1 each year.
The old law set a one-time deadline of January 1, 2026.
The new law names dual enrollment, work-based learning and apprenticeships as examples of off-campus activities that district rules must cover.
Dual enrollment means taking college classes while in high school.
units.note: plain-language definition, not from the cited sources

units.t: E-readers were dropped from the law's list of example devices, but that list is not complete.

subs.title: Other rules in the law

units.t: Districts and schools must set rules for off-campus activities like field trips, school transportation and sports.
Students learning online away from campus are not covered.
Schools can still give students laptops and tablets for schoolwork.
Schools are encouraged to hold family workshops, town halls and screen-free challenges.
Charter schools and other schools that can usually skip some state rules can't skip this one.
This tab compares three options.
Option A keeps the old law, House Bill 340 (2025), which covered only kindergarten through 8th grade.
Option B is House Bill (HB) 1009, which extends the ban to high schools and is now law.
Option C is a change, voted down by state senators, that would have let school districts allow phones between classes.

subs.title: If you care most about…

units.t: The two lines that follow use the same fall 2025 survey of 1,002 Georgia parents by the Emory Center for Child Health Policy, which surveys Georgia parents each year.

blocks.label: If you care most about your child's focus in class

units.t: In the Emory survey, the top reason parents cited for backing a high school cellphone ban was "Improved academic focus and learning."

blocks.label: If you care most about reaching your child in an emergency

units.t: In the Emory survey, the top reason parents cited for opposing a high school cellphone ban was "No way to reach child during emergency."
Option C, the change state senators voted down, has no line because we found no documented argument for it, and this guide does not recommend any option.

subs.title: Option A: Keep the old law (no state rule for high schools)

units.t: Sets a device ban for public school students in kindergarten through 8th grade only.
HB 1009, signed May 5, 2026, expands that law to high schools.
The new law takes effect Dec 31, 2026, and high schools must comply no later than July 1, 2027.
The law's new duties for districts and schools, such as a device policy every year, apply from Dec 31, 2026.
units.note: P-008 and P-014 set the duties, and P-019 sets the date the law takes effect

units.t: High school students and families keep whatever phone access their district allows.
units.note: the state rule covered only K-8 (P-006), so grades 9-12 were left to districts

units.t: In the Emory survey, 29.2% of parents opposed a high school ban.
Among those opponents, 74.8% cited having no way to reach their child in an emergency as a reason, 45.5% parental choice and 41.9% students' need to learn responsible use.
Fewer cited needing phones for health tools or apps (26.6%) or for schoolwork (19.8%).
Teacher Darryl Adams said high school students, who are older and often more independent, should be allowed to keep access to their phones.
High schools avoid new monitoring and enforcement duties, and districts keep deciding high school phone rules.
units.note: the duties come from P-014, and P-018 bars opting out

units.t: If the results of a 2025 Florida study apply here, students would also avoid the short-term rise in suspensions seen there, especially among Black students.
units.note: based on P-039 and P-055

units.t: In districts without limits, students can access phones in class, which the new law bans to reduce distractions.
units.note: the K-8-only rule (P-006) left grades 9-12 to districts; the law defines distraction-free education as banning access "to minimize distractions" (P-057)

units.t: State School Superintendent Richard Woods called for extending the ban "to end the harm caused by constant technology access and interruption."
A study of 12- to 15-year-olds in England found that strict school phone rules went with less phone and social media time during school, but found no evidence of better well-being.
That study couldn't test cause and effect.
units.note: it compared schools at one point in time (P-041)

units.t: If Florida's results apply here, students would miss the test-score gains found there in year two, and the drop in unexcused absences the study suggests.
units.note: based on P-040

units.t: High school rules could differ from one district to the next.
units.note: follows from leaving grades 9-12 to each district

units.t: Whether districts would have limited phones on their own.
State Sen. Sally Harrell said, "It has been done in high schools already, it’s been very successful and we look forward to rolling that out statewide."
We found no count of districts that already had limits.
units.note: none in the sources reviewed

subs.title: Option B: HB 1009 as passed (now law)

units.t: Bans device access for public high school students during the school day, a period the law calls "bell-to-bell": from the first bell to the last, including breaks and time between classes.
The bill passed the House 145 to 20 and the Senate 52 to 0, and the governor signed it on May 5, 2026.
The Florida study found that phone bans led to better test scores in the second year of the ban.
The study's findings also suggest the bans cut unexcused absences.
In the Emory survey, 70.8% of parents supported a high school ban.
Among those supporters, 87.7% cited better focus and learning as a reason, 71.2% better in-person social interactions, 69.1% better mental health and 60.3% better physical health and safety.
A study of 12- to 15-year-olds in England found that strict school phone rules went with less phone and social media time during school, but found no evidence of better well-being.
That study couldn't test cause and effect.
units.note: it compared schools at one point in time (P-041)

units.t: Families won't be able to reach students directly during the school day and will have to contact the school instead.
Of the 29.2% who opposed a ban, 74.8% cited having no way to reach their child in an emergency as a reason.

Students who use phones or smartwatches for health apps need an Individualized Education Program (IEP), Section 504 plan or medical plan that explicitly requires the device, unless another law requires access.
IEP and Section 504 plans are formal school plans for students with disabilities.
units.note: plain-language definition, not from the cited sources

units.t: Schools must set up phone storage, monitor and enforce the rules, review policies every year and keep families informed.
The law gives schools state guidance but sets aside no money.
units.note: no funding provision in the full enacted text, P-001 to P-019 and P-056 to P-061; P-016 provides guidance

units.t: Any state funding would come through the state budget, which we didn't review.
units.note: no funding provision in the law; the budget is outside our sources

units.t: The Florida study found that enforcing phone bans led to more suspensions in the short term, especially among Black students.
The rise in suspensions began to fade after the first year.
How much focus, learning and well-being will change in Georgia high schools, if at all, is not known yet.
units.note: the evidence so far is limited; see the Arguments tab

units.t: The same goes for suspensions and for reaching students in an emergency.

subs.title: Option C: The Senate amendment that failed

units.t: This proposed change, called an amendment, would have let districts allow high school students to access phones in the brief time between classes.
The amendment also rewrote the law's definition of the "bell-to-bell" period and left out "breaks", which the passed law includes.
Sen. Kemp of the 38th District offered the amendment, and it failed, 13 to 38.
This senator is not Gov. Brian Kemp.
units.note: P-027 identifies "Senator Kemp of the 38th"

units.t: In districts that chose to allow phones between classes, students and families could reach each other then.
units.note: inferred from the amendment text, P-027

units.t: Each district would decide for itself.
units.note: under P-027, access "may be permitted in accordance with policies" adopted by local school systems

units.t: In those districts, part of the school day would no longer be phone-free.
units.note: inferred from the amendment text, P-027

units.t: Whether phones between classes would change focus or learning compared with a full-day ban, since no source we reviewed measured this.
Supporters said the ban would cut distractions and ease anxiety.
Opponents said the ban could spark conflict for school staff and leave parents with fewer ways to reach their children in emergencies.
Below are three cards for the law and three against it, each with the same fields.

Our archived sources quote five people who spoke for the law: Gov. Brian Kemp; State School Superintendent Richard Woods; the bill's sponsor, state Rep. Scott Hilton; state Sen. Sally Harrell; and a student.
units.note: Gov. Kemp (P-029), Woods (P-036), Hilton as sponsor (P-028, P-051), Harrell (P-044) and a student (P-052)

units.t: The same sources quote one person who spoke against the law: teacher Darryl Adams.
units.note: Adams (P-047 to P-049)

units.t: Our sources also quote a public health professor who called parents' emergency concerns valid and said effective policies can address them with rapid parent notification and guaranteed access to phones when needed.
units.note: Gazmararian (P-037)

units.t: This count reflects whom those sources quoted, not how many people hold each view.

subs.title: How to read these cards

units.t: Every card uses the same fields, and one rule sets its evidence label.
units.note: labeling rule

units.t: "Supported" means the law's text or a study designed to show cause and effect backs the claim.
units.note: labeling rule

units.t: "Supported, with limits" means one such study backs the claim, but the support is narrow, such as a single working paper from another state with no Georgia results yet, and the label names those limits.
units.note: labeling rule

units.t: "Uncertain" means there are only statements, or studies that show links but not causes.
units.note: labeling rule

units.t: Values questions are marked as not mainly factual.
units.note: labeling rule

units.t: "Documented" means a real person made the argument, and we cite where.
units.note: labeling rule

units.t: A "predictive" claim is about what will happen; a "factual" claim is about what is true now.
units.note: labeling rule

units.t: Cards for the law come first, then cards against it; the order is not a ranking.
units.note: ordering rule

units.t: Several cards cite a fall 2025 survey of 1,002 Georgia parents by the Emory Center for Child Health Policy, which surveys Georgia parents each year.
Overall, 70.8% supported a high school ban and 29.2% opposed it.
For this question, the margin of error, or how far off the result is likely to be, is about 4 points either way.
units.note: 1.96 × 2.1 standard error (P-033) ≈ 4.1 percentage points

units.t: Reasons given within each group come from smaller samples.
units.note: each reason was asked only of parents who supported, or only of those who opposed, a ban (P-034, P-035)

units.t: Their margins of error are about 3.5 to 6 points for supporters' reasons and about 6 to 8 points for opponents' reasons.
Parents could give more than one reason.
units.note: the reasons in each table add up to more than 100% (P-034, P-035)

units.t: Two studies appear on the cards.
The Florida study is a 2025 working paper designed to estimate cause and effect.
A working paper is an early research report shared before formal publication.
units.note: plain-language definition, not from the cited sources

units.t: The Florida study compared students without running a randomized experiment.
units.note: P-038 names a "quasi-experimental" method; the plain-language meaning is ours

units.t: The Florida summary says the bans' effects were larger in middle and high schools, where more students own smartphones.
That summary doesn't say which effects were larger, or whether Florida's bans covered the whole school day, as Georgia's will.
units.note: the full abstract (P-067, P-038, P-068, P-039, P-040) doesn't say; Georgia's rule covers the whole day (P-002, P-007)

units.t: The English study surveyed 1,227 students ages 12 to 15 at 30 schools, using a standard well-being questionnaire.
The English study compared schools at one point in time, and its strict schools banned recreational phone use, meaning use for fun.
We read each study's summary, not the full paper.
units.note: process note

subs.title: 1. The ban will help students learn

units.t: Students would learn more with fewer distractions, supporters say.
A Florida study found phone bans led to better test scores in the ban's second year.
We found no measured results from Georgia high schools yet.
units.note: none in the sources reviewed, though a state senator said limits had been used in high schools already (P-046); Georgia's high school ban must start no later than July 1, 2027 (P-007)

units.t: Gov. Brian Kemp said the bills he signed would "reduce distractions in the classroom."
State School Superintendent Richard Woods said learning without distractions is "both an academic issue and a mental health issue."
Among parents who support a ban, 87.7% cited better focus and learning as a reason.
The Florida study found that phone bans led to better test scores in the second year, and its findings suggest they cut unexcused absences.
Fewer unexcused absences may explain a large share of the test-score gains.
The study's summary says the bans' effects were larger in middle and high schools, where more students own smartphones.
That summary doesn't say which effects were larger: test scores, absences or suspensions.
units.note: the full abstract (P-067, P-038, P-068, P-039, P-040) doesn't say

units.t: No one quoted in our sources disputed this claim directly.
units.note: none of the quoted statements argues that bans hurt learning

units.t: Of the 29.2% of parents who opposed a high school ban in the Emory survey, 19.8% cited "Phones needed for schoolwork" as a reason.
In the Florida study, the test-score gains came in the second year, after a first year in which suspensions rose.
The study used data from Florida only.
The study's summary doesn't describe how much of the school day the bans covered.
units.note: the full abstract (P-067, P-038, P-068, P-039, P-040) doesn't describe the bans' scope

units.t: The English study's summary reports no test-score results, and we didn't read the full paper.
units.note: its listed outcomes are well-being and phone and social media time (P-064)

units.t: Whether Georgia high schools will see results like Florida's, since we found no Georgia high school results yet.
units.note: none in the sources reviewed; Georgia's high school ban must start no later than July 1, 2027 (P-007)

cardMeta.evidence: Supported, with limits (one Florida working paper designed to estimate cause and effect; gains in year two; no Georgia results yet)

subs.title: 2. The ban will help teens' mental health and friendships

units.t: Teens' mental health and in-person social lives would improve, supporters say.
A study in England found no evidence of better well-being among 12- to 15-year-olds at schools that barred phone use for fun.
That study couldn't test cause and effect.
units.note: it compared schools at one point in time (P-041)

units.t: Woods called for extending the ban "to end the harm caused by constant technology access and interruption."
The bill's sponsor, state Rep. Scott Hilton, said, "The technology meant to bring people together actually makes us feel further apart."
Students testified in support at a legislative hearing; one, a 17-year-old, compared social media to cigarettes.
Among parents who support a ban, 71.2% cited better in-person social interactions and 69.1% better mental health as reasons.
Hilton said districts had reported less isolation among younger students under all-day phone limits.
In the English study, strict rules went with about 40 minutes less phone time and about 32 minutes less social media time during school.
units.note: 0.67 hours × 60 ≈ 40 minutes; 0.54 hours × 60 ≈ 32 minutes (P-042)

units.t: The English study's authors said there is "no evidence that restrictive school policies are associated with overall phone and social media use or better mental wellbeing in adolescents."

The authors added that their findings "do not provide evidence to support the use of school policies that prohibit phone use during the school day in their current form, and indicate that these policies require further development."
The English study also found no evidence of less phone or social media use overall at its strict schools.
The district reports Hilton described were about younger students.
The quoted passage gives no measurements behind those reports.
units.note: P-051 reports the claim without data

units.t: The English study can show links, not cause and effect, and its summary reports no results on friendships.
units.note: it compared schools at one point in time (P-041); its listed outcomes are in P-064

units.t: Whether, and how, the well-being and friendships of Georgia's public high school students will change.
No study we found measured well-being among American high school students under a full-day ban; the English study covered ages 12 to 15.
units.note: P-041, P-042, P-064; the Florida summary (P-038 to P-040) reports no well-being results

cardMeta.evidence: Uncertain (one study of 12- to 15-year-olds in England found no evidence of a well-being difference; it couldn't test cause and effect)

subs.title: 3. Phone bans are already working in Georgia

units.t: Younger students under phone limits in Georgia focus better and feel less isolated, and some high schools have had success, supporters say.
Our sources give statements, not measured results.
units.note: no data appears in P-028, P-046, P-051 or P-053

units.t: The governor's office said House Bill (HB) 1009 "builds on the success of HB 340," the 2025 law for kindergarten through 8th grade (K-8).

Hilton said districts had reported improved focus among younger students under all-day phone limits.

subs.title: 4. Families lose direct contact with students during the school day

units.t: Under the law, families must go through the school to reach students during the day.
Phones can be critical for families in an emergency, opponents say.
Our sources have no data on emergency safety.
units.note: no archived source reports how school alerts or students' own phones perform in emergencies

units.t: Among parents who oppose a ban, 74.8% cited having no way to reach their child in an emergency as a reason.
Teacher and parent Darryl Adams said phones can be critical for families seeking information during emergencies.
Under the law, parents who need to reach their child during the school day must contact the school directly.
The law has no emergency exception for students' own devices.
units.note: the full enacted text (P-001 to P-019, P-056 to P-061) allows access only under a plan that requires a device (P-013) or where access is "required by law" (P-007); neither is an emergency exception

units.t: Adams said that when two of his daughters were in a lockdown, he could not get updates for hours.
State Sen. Sally Harrell said, "We’ve gotten very dependent on being able to reach our kids whenever we want to, but that education time needs to be protected."

Julie Gazmararian, a professor at the Rollins School of Public Health, said, "Parents’ concerns about emergency access are valid and understandable. However, effective cellphone policies can address this by establishing rapid parent notification systems and guaranteed access to phones when needed."
The law requires each district's and school's policy to set clear protocols that send all emergency communication through school emergency systems, coordinated by school staff.
The law doesn't require the "rapid parent notification systems" or the "guaranteed access to phones when needed" that Gazmararian named, and her words don't say whose phones.

units.t: Districts can add faster parent alerts, because the law sets minimum rules, but by our reading they can't let students use their own phones in an emergency unless a student's disability or medical plan, or another law, requires access.

subs.title: 5. Enforcing the ban will burden school staff and can lead to conflict

units.t: Schools must enforce the ban.
Staff policing phones can invite conflict, opponents say.
A Florida study found enforcing bans led to more suspensions at first, especially among Black students.
We found no measured Georgia high school results or workload data.

units.t: Teacher Darryl Adams said he worries the bill would put the burden on teachers and administrators to police phones, a task that can invite conflict.
He said, "We have a lot of older teachers that do not want to have that confrontation."
Each school system must monitor and enforce the rules, which may include assigning staff and auditing phone storage.
Each district and school must also regularly review whether its rules work and adjust them as needed.
The law itself sets aside no money for these duties; any state funding would come through the budget, which we didn't review.

subs.title: 6. High school students should be allowed to keep phone access

units.t: High school students should be allowed to keep phone access, opponents say, because teens are older and often more independent and the choice should be parents'.
The disagreement is mainly about values.
Teacher Darryl Adams said high school students, who are older and often more independent, should be allowed to keep access to their phones.
Among parents who oppose a ban, 45.5% cited parental choice and 41.9% cited students' need to learn responsible use as reasons.
Among parents who oppose a ban, 26.6% cited needing phones for health tools or apps and 19.8% cited needing them for schoolwork.
Students testified in support of the ban, and a 17-year-old said, "Social media is the cigarette of our generation."
Most parents surveyed, 70.8%, supported a high school ban.

The law lets a student access a device that their Individualized Education Program (IEP), Section 504 plan or medical plan explicitly requires, but only "as necessary to fulfill the requirements" of that plan.
IEP and Section 504 plans are formal school plans for students with disabilities.
units.note: plain-language definition, not from the cited sources

units.t: Schools can also still provide laptops and tablets for schoolwork.
Our sources don't measure whether teens learn responsible phone use with or without a ban.
units.note: none of the archived sources addresses this

units.t: The disagreement here is mainly about who should decide and what school is for.

cardMeta.evidence: Not mainly a factual question (who should decide; whether teens learn responsible use with or without a ban is untested)

subs.title: Questions to weigh

units.t: What results would show whether the ban helps or hurts learning and well-being in Georgia high schools, and how soon could anyone know?
How well can school alert systems and students' own phones each keep families informed in an emergency, and how could anyone know?
Who would you want to set phone rules for high school students: the state, each school district or each family?

P-036.text: “Students’ ability to learn without distractions is both an academic issue and a mental health issue,” State School Superintendent Richard Woods said. “I hear this directly from students, parents, and educators, and this survey bears out what I’ve heard in those conversations. This is why we are calling for Georgia’s distraction-free legislation to be extended into grades 9-12, to end the harm caused by constant technology access and interruption.

P-037.text: “Parents’ concerns about emergency access are valid and understandable. P-038.text: In this study, we try to fill this gap by examining the causal effects of bans on student test scores, suspensions, and absences using detailed student-level data from Florida and a quasi-experimental research strategy relying upon differences in pre-ban cellphone use by students, as measured by building-level Advan data.

P-039.text: First, we show that the enforcement of cellphone bans in schools led to a significant increase in student suspensions in the short-term, especially among Black students, but disciplinary actions began to dissipate after the first year, potentially suggesting a new steady state after an initial adjustment period.

P-040.text: Second, we find significant improvements in student test scores in the second year of the ban after that initial adjustment period. Third, the findings suggest that cellphone bans in schools significantly reduce student unexcused absences, an effect that may explain a large fraction of the test score gains. The effects of cellphone bans are more pronounced in middle and high school settings where student smartphone ownership is more common.

P-055.text: David N. Figlio and Umut Özek, "The Impact of Cellphone Bans in Schools on Student Outcomes: Evidence from Florida," NBER Working Paper 34388 (2025), https://doi.org/10.3386/w34388.

P-041.text: We conducted a cross-sectional observational study with adolescents from 30 English secondary schools, comprising 20 with restrictive (recreational phone use is not permitted) and 10 with permissive (recreational phone use is permitted) policies.

P-042.text: We recruited 1227 participants (age 12–15) across 30 schools. Mean WEMWBS score was 47 (SD = 9) with no evidence of a difference between groups (adjusted mean difference −0.48, 95% CI −2.05 to 1.06, p = 0.62). Adolescents attending schools with restrictive, compared to permissive policies had lower phone (adjusted mean difference −0.67 h, 95% CI −0.92 to −0.43, p = 0.00024) and social media time (adjusted mean difference −0.54 h, 95% CI −0.74 to −0.36, p = 0.00018) during school time, but there was no evidence for differences when comparing usage time on weekdays or weekends.

P-043.text: There is no evidence that restrictive school policies are associated with overall phone and social media use or better mental wellbeing in adolescents. The findings do not provide evidence to support the use of school policies that prohibit phone use during the school day in their current form, and indicate that these policies require further development.

P-054.text: Cairo High School June 1, 2026 Georgia House Bill 1009 is a law signed by Governor Brian Kemp that enacts a "bell-to-bell" ban on personal electronic devices for public high school students. The legislation requires high schools to restrict the use of devices like smartphones, smartwatches, tablets, and headphones during the instructional school day. Cairo High School will begin implementation of this law in the 2026-2027 school year.

P-070.text: Each year, the Emory Center for Child Health Policy, based in the Rollins School of Public Health, surveys Georgia parents to understand their concerns about their children.

P-071.text: Supporters argued the move would cut distractions and ease anxiety, while opponents warned it could spark conflict for school staff and leave parents with fewer ways to reach their children during emergencies.

P-072.text: Under the new measure, restrictions for high school students would begin in the 2027-28 school year.

verification.intro: On Nov 8, 2026, this page was rewritten for readers new to the subject, after usability feedback: it now says what the law means for students, families and staff, and what each side says it protects. An AI agent wrote it from saved copies of its sources. Separate AI checkers, which never saw the drafting, then checked it in rounds. In this trial, no person checked the facts. Here is what the checkers did, what they found, and what is still open.

sections.title: What we checked
paras: Each round runs the same checks. A page passes a round only when every check passes. After that, we fix only sentences that misstate a source or break our writing rules, and fresh checkers look again at just those sentences: one for facts, and one that asks of each changed summary line whether we would write it the same way about the other side. Other suggestions wait for the next full round.
head: Check
What it does
Pass mark
rows: Code confirms that every sentence cites a source passage or is labeled as our analysis, that quotes match word for word, that saved files match their fingerprints, and that the reading level is about grade 8 or lower.
A separate AI checker sees only this page and the source passages. For each sentence it must copy the exact words that support it, and code confirms those words are really there.

Three more AI checkers. One speaks up for the law's supporters, one for its critics, and a neutral editor checks the rules. The editor also asks of each sentence: would we write it the same way about the other side?
Both side reviewers give at least 4 of 5, and no serious problem

Each round, we hid errors in a copy of the page, such as a wrong deadline, an exception the law doesn't make, a misquoted survey answer and a sentence recommending an option. The fact-checker had to find them without knowing they were there.

sections.title: What each round found
paras: No fact-check found a claim that its sources didn't support, only sentences that said more than the sources did. Rounds 1 to 4 checked earlier versions. Round 5 checked the rewrite for new readers, and round 6 checked one evidence label that all three panelists asked us to change.

sections.title: What's still open
paras: These suggestions change a card, a label or the balance between sides, so they wait for the next full round. Some contradict each other; we list both views rather than pick one quietly.
items: Reviewers disagree on two evidence labels: supporters want card 2's and card 5's labels worded differently; critics accept them. Labels change only in a full round.
Card 2's title says "friendships"; the survey's words are "in-person social interactions". Titles change only in a full round.
The K-8 line notes the law dropped e-readers from its list of examples; the law's general definition may still cover them.
Our sources give no phone number or email for lawmakers or school districts, so the page can't list them.
The State School Superintendent's job isn't described in any source we saved.

sections.title: What this can't do
paras: All the checkers are AI, like the writer, so they may share blind spots. Hiding test errors measures only the kinds of errors we thought to hide.
The checkers compare this page with the sources we saved. They can't tell what is missing from those sources.
The two side reviewers stand in for real people's views. They are not real people.
